''Taxodium huegelii'' C.Lawson{{Cite web|title=Taxodium huegelii C.Lawson — The Plant List|url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/record/kew-2516542|access-date=2020-09-20|website=www.theplantlist.org}} | synonyms_ref = {{cite web |url= http://www.conifers.org/cu/Taxodium_mucronatum.php |title=Taxodium mucronatum |publisher=The Gymnosperm Database |access-date= 2009-10-12}} | range_map = Taxodium mucronatum range map.png | range_map_caption = Natural range }} '''''Taxodium mucronatum''''', commonly known as '''Montezuma bald cypress''',{{PLANTS|id=TAMU|taxon=Taxodium mucronatum|access-date=8 December 2015}} '''Montezuma cypress''',{{GRIN | access-date = 2020-02-04}} '''{{lang|es|sabino}}''',{{cite web |title=Montezuma baldcypress |url=http://texastreeid.tamu.edu/content/treedetails/?id=122 |work=Trees of Texas |publisher=[[Texas A&M Forest Service]] |access-date=28 November 2025}} or '''{{lang|es|ahuehuete}}''', is a [[Conifer|coniferous]] tree in the family [[Cupressaceae]]. It is primarily native to [[Mexico]] and [[Guatemala]], with a few populations in the southwestern United States.{{cite journal |url=http://www.fao.org/docrep/l2015e/l2015e05.htm |title=Guatemalan Conifers |first=Thomas T. |last=Veblen |author-link=Thomas T. Veblen |journal=Unasylva |volume=29 |issue=118 |year=1977 |publisher=Food and Agriculture Organization |access-date=2009-10-14}} {{lang|es|Ahuehuete}} is derived from the [[Nahuatl language|Nahuatl]] name for the tree, '''{{lang|nah|āhuēhuētl}}''', which means 'upright drum in water'{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-IDsW8YmaigC |title=Introduction to Classical Nahuatl |first=James Richard |last=Andrews |publisher=University of Oklahoma Press |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-8061-3452-9 |page=328}} or 'old man of the water'. ==Description== It is a large [[evergreen]] or [[semi-evergreen]] tree growing to {{convert|40|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall and with a trunk of {{convert|1|-|3|m|ft|abbr=on}} diameter (occasionally much more; see below). The [[leaf|leaves]] are spirally arranged but twisted at the base to lie in two horizontal ranks, {{convert|1|-|2|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|1|-|2|mm|in|abbr=on}} broad. The [[conifer cone|cones]] are ovoid, {{convert|1.5|-|2.5|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|1|-|2|cm|in|abbr=on}} broad. Unlike [[Taxodium distichum|bald cypress]] and [[Taxodium ascendens|pond cypress]], Montezuma cypress rarely produces [[cypress knee]]s from the roots. Trees from the Mexican highlands achieve a notable stoutness. One specimen, the [[Árbol del Tule]] in [[Santa María del Tule, Oaxaca]], Mexico, is the [[List of superlative trees#Stoutest|stoutest tree]] in the world with a diameter of {{convert|11.42|m|ft|abbr=on}}. Several other specimens from {{convert|3|-|6|m|ft|abbr=on}} diameter are known. The second stoutest tree in the world is [[Sunland Baobab|the Big Baobab]], an [[Adansonia digitata|African baobab]]. ==Distribution and habitat== [[File:Montezuma Bald Cypress (Taxodium mucronatum), Rio Pilón near Villagrán, Municipality of Villagrán, Tamaulipas, Mexico (9 August 2005).jpg|left|thumb|Montezuma bald cypress (''Taxodium mucronatum''), growing on the Rio Pilón near Villagrán, Municipality of Villagrán, Tamaulipas, Mexico (9 August 2005)]] Montezuma cypress is primarily a [[Riparian zone|riparian]] tree, growing along upland riversides, but can also be found next to [[Spring (hydrosphere)|springs]] and marshes. It occurs from {{convert|300|to|2500|m|ft|abbr=on}}, in Mexico mainly in highlands at {{convert|1600|-|2300|m|ft|abbr=on}} in altitude. ''T. mucronatum'' is very [[drought]]-tolerant and fast-growing{{cite journal |url=http://arnoldia.arboretum.harvard.edu/pdf/articles/2011-69-2-can-taxodium-be-improved.pdf |title=Can ''Taxodium'' Be Improved? |first=David |last=Creech |author2=Lijing Zhou |author3=Yin Yunlong |author4=Teobaldo Eguiluz-Piedra |journal=Arnoldia |publisher=Arnold Arboretum of Harvard University |date=November 2011 |volume=69 |issue=2 |pages=11–20 |doi=10.5962/p.258700 |archive-date=2019-11-25 |access-date=2017-12-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191125024551/http://arnoldia.arboretum.harvard.edu/pdf/articles/2011-69-2-can-taxodium-be-improved.pdf }} and favors climates that are rainy throughout the year or at least with high summer rainfall. ''Taxodium mucronatum'' is native to much of Mexico as far south as the highlands of southern Mexico. Two [[Disjunct distribution|disjunct]] populations exist in the United States. One is in the [[Lower Rio Grande Valley|Rio Grande Valley]] of southernmost [[Texas]], while the other is in southern [[New Mexico]], near [[Las Cruces, New Mexico|Las Cruces]].{{cite web |url=http://plantanswers.com/Library/ViewQuestion.asp?QuestionID=1531 |first=Michael Martin |last=Melendrez |title=Search for the Answer |publisher=PLANTanswers.com |access-date=2017-12-09}}{{cite journal |url=http://hortsci.ashspublications.org/content/34/3/459.4 |first=Rolston St. |last=Hilaire |title=105 Propagation of ''Taxodium mucronatum'' (Montezuma Cypress) |journal=HortScience |year=1999 |volume=34 |issue=3 |page=459|doi=10.21273/HORTSCI.34.3.459D |doi-access=free }} Within [[Guatemala]], the tree is restricted to [[Huehuetenango Department]]. ==Culture== in 1910.{{cite journal |url=http://arnoldia.arboretum.harvard.edu/pdf/articles/475.pdf |title=El Arbol del Tule: The Ancient Giant of Oaxaca |first=Zsolt |last=Debreczy |author2=István Rácz |journal=Arnoldia |publisher=Arnold Arboretum of Harvard University |date=Winter 1997–1998 |volume=57 |issue=4 |pages=3–11 |archive-date=2010-08-01 |access-date=2009-10-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100801163959/http://arnoldia.arboretum.harvard.edu/pdf/articles/475.pdf }} The tree is sacred to the [[Indigenous peoples in Mexico|native peoples of Mexico]], and is featured in the [[Zapotec civilization#Religion|Zapotec]] [[Mesoamerican creation myths|creation myth]].{{cite web |url=http://plantconservatory.calpoly.edu/Tree/Taxodium_mucronatum.html |title=''Taxodium mucronatum'' Montezuma Bald Cypress |work=Cal Poly Plant Conservatory |publisher=California Polytechnic State [[Aztec]]s, the combined shade of an {{lang|nah|āhuēhuētl}} and a {{lang|nah|pōchōtl}} (''[[Ceiba pentandra]]'') metaphorically represented a ruler's authority.{{cite web |url=http://whp.uoregon.edu/Lockhart/HaskettTitulos.pdf |first=Robert |last=Haskett |title=Primordial Titles |year=2007 |work=Sources and Methods for the Study of Postconquest Mesoamerican web|url=https://mexicanroutes.com/did-hernan-cortes-really-cry-at-the-tree-of-sorrows/|title=Did Hernán Cortés really cry at the Tree of Sorrows?|website=mexicanroutes.com|date=23 October 2023 |access-date=2023-10-23}} [[Hernán Cortés]] wept under an ahuehuete in [[Popotla]]{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qDUCAAAAYAAJ |first=John Lewis |last=Geiger |title=A Peep at Mexico: Narrative of a Journey Across the Republic from the Pacific to the Gulf in December 1873 and January 1874 |publisher=Trübner and Co. |year=1874 |page=268}} after suffering defeat during the [[La Noche Triste|Battle of La Noche Triste]].{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tvk5FN3L-Q0C |first=Richard Stephen |last=Felger |author2=Matthew Brian Johnson |author3=Michael Francis Wilson |title=The Trees of Sonora, Mexico |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-19-512891-8 |page=41}} This plant is mentioned in the 2015 short story "Rivers" by [[John Keene (writer)|John Keene]], which reimagines the story of [[Mark Twain]]'s ''[[Adventures of Huckleberry Finn]]''.{{Cite book|title=Counternarritives|last=Keene|first=John|publisher=New Directions|year=2015|location=New York|page=235}} ==Uses== [[File:Ahuehuetes en Chapultepec.jpg|thumb|An 1875 painting, ''Ahuehuetes en Chapultepec'', by [[José María Velasco Gómez]] depicting the cypress by the lake in [[Chapultepec]].]] Montezuma cypresses have been used as [[Ornamental plant|ornamental trees]] since [[Pre-Columbian]] times. The Aztecs planted {{lang|nah|āhuēhuētl}} along processional paths in the gardens of [[Chapultepec]] because of its association with government.{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dmclFThar_UC |editor=Michel Conan W. John Kress |first=Susan Toby |last=Evans |title=Botanical Progress, Horticultural Innovation and Cultural Changes |volume=28 |publisher=Dumbarton Oaks |year=2007 |isbn=978-0-88402-327-2 |page=90}} [[Artificial island]]s called {{lang|es|[[chinampa]]s}} were formed in the shallow lakes of the [[Valley of Mexico]] by adding soil to rectangular areas enclosed by trees such as {{lang|nah|āhuēhuētl}}; they also lined the region's canals prior to [[Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire|Spanish conquest]]. Ahuehuetes are frequently cultivated in Mexican parks and gardens. The wood is used to make house beams and furniture,. The Aztecs used its resin to treat [[gout]], [[peptic ulcer|ulcer]]s, skin diseases, wounds, and toothaches. A [[decoction]] made from the bark was used as a [[diuretic]] and an [[emmenagogue]]. [[Pitch (resin)|Pitch]] derived from the wood was used as a cure for [[bronchitis]] The leaves acted as a relaxant and could help reduce itching.{{cite web |url=http://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/tree/taxmuc/all.html |title=Taxodium mucronatum |first=Janet |last=Sullivan |year=1994 |work=Fire Effects Information System |publisher=United States Forest Service |access-date=2009-10-13}} In some parts of Mexico the foliage is used to decorate church altars during religious ceremonies.{{cite web |title=Taxodium mucronatum |url=https://www.iucnredlist.org/species/34029/2840943 |website=IUCN Red List of Threatened Species |publisher=International Union for Conservation of Nature |access-date=7 July 2022}} [[John Naka]], a [[bonsai]] master, donated his very first bonsai, a Montezuma cypress, to the National Bonsai and Penjing Museum of the United States. {{Citation needed|date=February 2023}} A linear grove is located in the main courtyard of the [[Getty Center]] Art Museum, thriving since 1995.{{cite news |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1997-dec-14-re-63912-story.html |title=A Gardener's Getty
